abstract: Escherichia coli employs stress responses to maintain homeostasis and mitigate harmful impacts on cellular and genomic integrity. Two key systems managing tolerance to unfavorable conditions include the DNA damage-inducible SOS response and the oxidative stress-inducible OxyR response. Recently, we demonstrated that simultaneous activation of these two systems resulted in the suppression of the SOS-associated hypermutability, suggesting that these systems when co-induced may yield new regulatory features. To further investigate these systems individually and jointly we used whole-transcriptome sequencing and proteomics to assess the underlying gene and protein networks. We used E. coli K-12 strain MG1655 and its derivatives carrying the recA730 and oxyR2c alleles that yield constitutive expression of the SOS and OxyR systems, respectively. Our findings indicate the genetic scope of these systems to be significantly broader than previously reported, revealing scores of differentially expressed genes not formerly classified as part of the systems (143 in the recA730 and 248 in the oxyR2c strain). A key finding was that the constitutive co-expression of the two systems led to a broad suppression of genes of both systems. Importantly, a novel group of 137 genes not belonging to either individual system proved differentially expressed under co-activation conditions, which was further corroborated by proteomic data. Overall, the data suggest that SOS-induced cells may be preoccupied with aerobic energy producing activities, while OxyR-induced cells are focused on energy-conserving reactions, biofilm formation and reducing motility. Under co-activating conditions a compromise might be reached that represents a further adaptive mechanism to support survival under multi-stress conditions.
